1:
Clarke gives the shape of the chapter: the prophet forbidden to encumber himself with a wife and family or to share in the small joys and sorrows of his neighbours, which were to be absorbed in the public calamity; then the sins that would draw it down; then a restoration intimated; then the conversion of the Gentiles foretold. Ellicott says the formula introduces a new and distinct message, more terrible in its threatenings than any before it, and though nothing in its contents fixes the date he thinks of it as near the close of a particular reign, when the king was trusting to an Egyptian alliance and the people taunted the prophet with the non-fulfilment of his predictions. Gill is less sure, thinking it more probably a continuation, and notes the introduction is omitted in two ancient versions.

Henry makes the whole a sign. They would not regard what the prophet said; let it be tried whether they will regard what he does. In everything he must conduct himself as one who expected to see his country in ruins shortly, and so must show that he is himself satisfied of the truth of what few regarded when he predicted it. Others go on in their usual course, but he forbears marriage and mourning and mirth. Those who would convince others of the word of God, Henry says, must make it appear even in the most self-denying instances that they believe it themselves; if we would rouse others out of their security and persuade them to sit loose to the world, we must ourselves be mortified to present things.

Calvin puts the prohibition on the broadest possible ground. The law of the creation of man was to increase and multiply, and since mankind is perpetuated by marriage, God here shows that this land was unworthy of the common and general blessing enjoyed by the whole race; it is as if he had said that they live as yet but a quick destruction awaits them, for he will deprive them of the favour he has hitherto shown to all mankind. In the person of the prophet, Calvin says, God meant to show the Jews that they deserved to be exterminated from the earth. He raises the question whether the prophet was in fact unmarried, and answers that it does not matter, since the command was received in a vision and might have been proclaimed either way; yet he thinks it probable that he was, since like the walking naked and the yoke carried on the neck his celibacy might have been meant as a living representation. He also warns that celibacy is not commended here, as some foolish men have imagined from the passage. Ellicott adds what the words would have meant to an Israelite and a priest, for whom marriage was not only a happiness but a duty, so that to be cut off from it was to renounce both. Gill and Clarke make the plainer point that a family would have been inconvenient and the calamity more bearable alone.

The deaths themselves are read as lingering rather than sudden. Gill renders the phrase deaths of diseases or sicknesses, by which a man consumes gradually and is not snatched away at once. Calvin makes the same distinction the point: they are not threatened with a common kind of death but with continual languor causing them to pine away in the greatest pain, sudden death being more tolerable, as one psalmist complains that the ungodly have no bands in their death. Ellicott notes that among a people who attached such importance to funeral rites the neglect of them was a symptom of extremest misery, and cites a Latin poet on a plague in which the customed rites of sepulture were no longer practised in the city, and a Greek historian on the plague at Athens.
5:
The house of mourning is really a mourning-feast, and everyone says so. Ellicott notes the word is found only here and in one other place, where it is rendered banquet, that the Latin gives house of feasting and the Greek a drinking party, and that the root means a shout, applicable to joy or sorrow alike, the context deciding for sorrow though the idea of a gathering should be recognised. Gill reports the same range, one authority deriving it from an Arabic word for lifting the voice in weeping or joy and another glossing it a feast. Calvin agrees that such feasts were made when anyone died and renders the phrase literally, enter not the house of shouting.

On the withdrawal Ellicott takes the word peace in its highest power, as including all other blessings: it is the peace of God, once given and now withheld, and men were to accept that withdrawal in silent awe rather than with the conventional routine of customary sorrow. Keil and Delitzsch call the saying fearfully solemn. Calvin insists the prohibition is not about moderating private grief, since the subject is not the personal feeling of the prophet; God is declaring the land so desolate that hardly one would survive to mourn the dead.

The cutting and the baldness were forbidden by the law, as Clarke and Ellicott both note, probably to mark Israel off from the nations round; and both observe that the practices were nevertheless common. Clarke describes them, the tearing of hair, the rending of garments, the cutting of hands and arms and faces, and adds that these were not only signs of sorrow but were supposed to ease the dead and appease angry deities. Ellicott thinks the shaving of the crown was the commoner of the two. Calvin is careful that the prophet does not mention them by way of commendation, nor suppose the people were keeping the law in this respect, since God had forbidden them to imitate corrupt customs. Wesley makes the grim practical point that men shall die so fast they shall have no leisure for it.

One verb is disputed. Ellicott says the marginal reading, neither shall men break bread for them, gives the true meaning, and describes the custom it points to: after the first burst of sorrow and fasting, friends came to comfort the mourner, and a feast was prepared of the bread of mourners and the cup of consolation. Calvin works the text out at length: three ancient versions must have read bread rather than for them, the two words differ by very little, and though only two manuscripts support it he inclines to think it the true reading, since the verb before it and the correspondence between bread and drink in the two halves require it. Gill gives both, the stretching or wringing of hands and the breaking of bread. Wesley describes the sending of meat and wine to the bereaved. Ellicott adds a suggestion none of the others make, that some reference to this practice may be implied in the blessing of the bread and the cup at the Last Supper, so that in giving the symbols of his death the Lord was keeping his own funeral feast with his disciples.

The house of feasting follows the other, as Ellicott puts it: if the prophet might not enter the house of mourning, much more must he hold aloof from mirth, standing apart in the awful consciousness of his solitary mission. Calvin gives the reason more harshly, that every intercourse with this people is accursed, so that he must be their associate neither in joy nor in sorrow. Clarke describes the mingled wine given to the deepest in distress to divert their minds, a custom he says was common among almost all nations. Gill notes the prophet had attended such feasts at other times, and that his abstaining was itself the sign.
10:
Henry allows two readings of the question and prefers the harsher. One would hope, he says, that some asked it with a humble penitent heart, wanting to know the sin for which God contended with them so that they might cast it away: show us the Jonah that raises the storm and we will throw it overboard. But it seems rather the language of those who quarrelled at the word and challenged God to show what they had done to deserve such severity; instead of humbling and condemning themselves they stand on their own justification, insinuating that they were wronged. It is amazing, Henry adds, how hardly sinners are brought to justify God and judge themselves in trouble. Ellicott says the threatenings are met with real or affected wonder, and that all the prophets had more or less to encounter the same hardness. Calvin calls it blindness and even madness not to examine themselves when smitten, conscience being to them like a thousand witnesses; hardly one in a hundred submitted.

The answer begins with the fathers, and Calvin thinks the verses have been divided wrongly: were the latter part of the eleventh joined to the twelfth, the apparent repetition would disappear. He gives his own rendering, setting the conduct of the fathers in the first part and the conduct of fathers and children together in the second, the worse conduct of the children being that they did not hearken to the voice of God by his prophets. He is careful about the principle: punishment would not have fallen on the children except that they followed the wickedness of their fathers, though the scripture often declares that children are punished with their fathers, because God will at some time require an account of all sins. Clarke states the same limit in one sentence, that the sins of the fathers would not have been visited on the children had they not followed the example and become even worse.

Why the children are called worse is then explained. Calvin says sins become worse before God when children strengthen themselves in wickedness by following the examples of their fathers, and that these had not only the law set before them but prophets sent repeatedly with reproofs, so that what was punished so severely was their obstinacy: they imitated their wicked fathers and then not merely despised but rejected every warning. Gill puts it that they committed the same sins with more aggravating circumstances, wilfully and impudently and obstinately. Ellicott corrects a single word, that the imagination of the English is better rendered stubbornness.

The sentence is that they shall serve other gods in a land they do not know, and Ellicott hears bitter irony in it: you have chosen to serve the gods of other nations here in your own land, and by a righteous retribution you shall serve them in another sense, in bondage to their worshippers, with no respite night or day; he would also render the last clause since rather than where. Calvin rejects the softer reading. Some mitigate the words as meaning only the servitude of being subject to idolaters, but he thinks that too remote: God abandoned them because they had violated pure worship, and it is probable they were forced into ungodly ceremonies when the Chaldeans could treat them as slaves without any measure of humanity, and even constrained to it by way of sport, their conquerors triumphing over them daily. Gill reads the calling out as being taken by force and against their wills, since having cast off the Lord it was just that they should be cast off by him.
14:
The turn is marked by a single word, and its force is disputed. Gill reports three renderings, therefore, or notwithstanding their sins and the punishment brought for them, or surely, one authority taking it as an oath by which God swore he would redeem them though they had behaved so ill. Wesley reads it simply as sweetening: God softens the dreadful threatenings that precede with a comfortable promise of restoration. Henry warns that mercy and judgment are so interwoven in these verses that it is hard to know to which some of the passages belong, and that some seem to look as far forward as the times of the gospel.

Calvin will not have it as consolation only, and says so against the common exposition. The passage is commonly expounded as though a comfort were interposed in which the faithful alone are concerned; he considers it mixed, the prophet speaking in part in severe terms of the dreadful exile he foretells and in part blending some consolation, the latter referred to only indirectly. What the verse chiefly does, on his reading, is amplify the threat. They knew how cruel the servitude was from which their fathers had been delivered, a condition worse than a hundred deaths, when they were driven to servile works and all justice was denied them and their offspring were put to death from the womb; so the comparison shows more fully what a dreadful punishment awaited them, since their redemption would be much more incredible. It is as though he had said that they know from what their fathers came out, from a brazen furnace and as it were from the depth of death, a redemption to be remembered to the end of the world; but God will now cast them into an abyss deeper than that of Egypt.

Calvin then gives the reason the later deliverance will be the greater miracle: there will be less hope remaining, when the Chaldeans have subdued and scattered them like a body torn asunder, when the name of Israel is extinguished, the worship of God subverted and the temple destroyed; when all things appear past remedy, that captivity will be far more dreadful than the one their fathers suffered, and the restoration from it far more remarkable. Gill reaches a similar conclusion by a different route, that the hardships in Babylon were in some respects greater and the favour recent and fresh, so that it would swallow up the memory of the older mercy, which would be comparatively forgotten. Clarke states it plainly, that the deliverance from the northern land will be as remarkable as the deliverance of their fathers from Egypt.

One small curiosity is preserved. Gill reports that the Jews gathered from the word brought up, or caused to ascend, that the land of Israel was higher than all other lands, since men are said to go up to it out of Egypt and out of every other country alike.
16:
Who the fishers and hunters are is the question of the passage, and the answers run in two directions. Gill lists five: the Egyptians, who lived much on fish; the Chaldeans, whom he prefers, who besieged Jerusalem and took the people as fish in a net; the Medes and Persians who searched them out to send them home; a later leader persuading the captives to return; and the apostles, fishers by occupation, whom Christ made fishers of men. Ellicott is firm that the words refer to the threat and not to the promise, the fishers being the invading nations surrounding the country as with a drag-net and letting none escape; the application either to the gathering of the dispersed or to the later preachers of the gospel is, he says, an after-thought whose source is the saying about fishers of men, though he allows that saying may itself have been suggested by this passage.

Calvin is blunter, calling the apostle reading wholly foreign to the subject, and gives his reasons. Those who take it so assume the previous verse promised a near deliverance, which he has already rejected; and even if that were granted, it would not follow that the same subject continues, since the prophet immediately returns to threatenings; the allegory of hunters and fishers is too remote for a promise, and the mention of hills and mountains makes it plainer still. He connects the whole plainly: having said the coming evil would be worse than the Egyptian bondage, the prophet confirms it, the Chaldeans going through the whole land like fishers so as to leave none but the most ignoble, whom they afterwards took away too; and he reports that some distinguish the fishers as those who slew the conquered by the sword and the hunters as those disposed to spare and drive into exile. Ellicott makes the distinction differently, the fishers standing for the main body of the army and the hunters for the irregular skirmisher, since men might take refuge in the caves of the rocks as hunted beasts do and be driven even from these; Keil and Delitzsch say the same of those who had taken refuge in the mountains and ravines. Ellicott adds that a Greek historian describes this very process of drag-netting a country as practised by a great army on the islands.

The all-seeing eyes are read by Calvin as doctrine attached to prophecy. The prophets were not endued with the Spirit merely to foretell things to come, which would have been very jejune, but added the causes; so a doctrine is added here as a seasoning, that the destruction was at hand because the people had long provoked God. Since there is no end to the evasions of hypocrites, God reminds them that he knows their iniquities and is a fit judge, so that they contend in vain to excuse or extenuate. Gill and Ellicott both take the eyes on the severer side, of ways that cannot be hidden.

The recompence double divides them three ways. Ellicott gives a legal sense: restitution to double the amount of the wrong was almost the normal standard of punishment under the law, so the words threaten full punishment at the utmost rigour, and he sets against it the brighter use of the same thought elsewhere, where Israel having received double for all her sins may now hope for mercy. Gill and Wesley both deny that double means twice what the sins deserved, taking it rather as full and abundant measure after a long forbearance. Calvin takes the word rendered first as meaning from the beginning, and reads the whole as God gathering the long-buried iniquities of fathers and children into one bundle. On the carcasses Clarke and Ellicott give the same two options, the lifeless idols themselves or the bodies of the victims sacrificed to them.
19:
Calvin explains why the chapter breaks off into prayer. What had been said might seem contrary to the promises and subversive of the covenant made with Abraham: God had chosen one people out of the whole world, and now that this people were trodden underfoot even the most perfect of the faithful might suppose the covenant void. This was a most grievous trial, enough to shake the strongest minds, and the prophet returns to it here to forestall it, turning to God and speaking of the calling of the Gentiles, which was enough to remove the stumbling-block entirely. Calvin draws a rule from the turn: it shows what is best done in a dark state of things, since Satan hunts for nothing more than to involve us in intricate disputes, being an acute disputant and a sophist, and we are too ready to receive what he suggests, so that there is no better remedy than to break off such disputes and turn our eyes elsewhere. Gill describes the same movement as the prophet casting off impatience and unbelief; Ellicott hears in the words an echo of several psalms; and Keil and Delitzsch note that the prophet does not disclose what led him to think of the heathen, though it may be gathered from what precedes.

The vision of the Gentiles is read the same way by all. Clarke takes it as a prediction of their calling and a light amid much darkness, since in such dismal accounts there is need of some gracious promise about an amended state of the world. Ellicott sharpens it into a contrast: in that far-off time of which other prophets had spoken the Gentiles should come, turning from the vanities they had inherited, while Israel, who had inherited a truer faith, was abasing herself to their level or below, answering in the affirmative a question that seemed to admit only of a negative.

That question is where Calvin does his best work. Some, he says, explain the verse frigidly, as though the point were only that men are doubly foolish to form gods from wood or gold, since these cannot change their nature and the stone remains a stone. But the prophet reasons differently: can he who is not God make a god, can the created be the creator? No one can give what he has not, and there is in man no divine power. The argument is drawn from what is absurd, so that men might acknowledge not merely their presumption but their monstrous madness; for anyone asked about his condition must confess that he is a creature, an ephemeral animal whose life is like a shadow. God does not create a god; he creates men and angels and the heavens and the earth, but does not put forth his power to create a new god. Gill and Clarke put the same absurdity as questions, whether a mortal man can put deity into gold or wood.

The last verse returns to threat. Calvin notes the demonstrative particle showing the near approach of vengeance, and takes the words as intimating that the exile would be an extraordinary event far exceeding any that preceded it. He also argues that the therefore infers from both the captivity and the restoration, since the restoration was as remarkable an interposition as the captivity if not more so, and the later preservation of the people from idolatry is to be ascribed to the power shown in both. Clarke reads it as fixed purpose, that nothing shall prevent the visitation, and that since they would not receive the abundance of mercies they shall learn what the true God can do in judgment. Wesley says they shall know that the name is one who has his being from himself. Gill alone reads the verse forward, of the Gentiles being made to know the true God through the gospel.
